implementation_notes: The futures crate supplies the shareable completion handle: FutureExt::shared() turns a future into a cloneable Shared whose output must be Clone and which many tasks may await; a Tokio Mutex (or std Mutex) guarded HashMap<K, Shared<Fut>> is the registry, with the entry inserted before the work is polled and removed when the flight ends. singleflight-async packages exactly this contract - SingleFlight::work(key, fn) runs 'only one operation in-flight at a given moment' and duplicate callers wait for and return the same value - and tokio::sync::OnceCell covers the single-slot case where one key is enough. What replaces the classic structure is therefore a Shared future plus an async-aware registry rather than a hand-written wait queue.
pitfalls: Never hold a std::sync::Mutex guard across .await: the guard is not Send and a task holding it cannot be spawned; scope the lock or use tokio::sync::Mutex.
shared() requires Output: Clone, so errors must be cloneable too (wrap them in Arc) - one shared error instance is delivered to every waiter.

A Shared future is driven by whoever polls it: if every clone is dropped before completion the underlying computation is cancelled, so the leader must keep its own handle (or an owning task) alive until the flight finishes.
Remove the entry when the flight ends (a drop guard around the registry entry) or completed flights accumulate and the map becomes a cache.
Cancelling one waiter's task must not cancel the shared handle: keep the flight in a task of its own and have waiters await clones of the handle.
